evidence_timeline.summary: We crossmatched all public TNS transients (about 187,000 in the VLASS footprint) with the CIRADA VLASS Quick Look epoch 1 and epoch 2 component catalogs, classifying each radio-coincident transient by the timing of its VLASS subtile observations relative to the optical discovery. A shifted-position control yields about 10 chance matches per epoch against about 2,500 real ones. After archival radio vetting (FIRST/NVSS) and multi-archive characterization (Legacy DR10 host offsets, SDSS spectra, NEOWISE, ZTF light curves), we report 5 unclassified candidates (5 emergent, 0 fading) whose nuclear 3 GHz radio state changed within a window containing the optical event. The method blindly recovers both AT 2020aboe (AstroNote 2026-209) and the published repeating partial TDE AT 2020vdq as its top-ranked known objects. Spectroscopic and radio follow-up of the candidates is encouraged; all data products are available on request.

evidence_timeline.summary: We report AT 2020afkm, a dust-obscured mid-infrared transient in NGC 3239 (about 7-12 Mpc), found in a blind difference-imaging search of the unWISE time-resolved coadds of 318 nearby galaxies. Quiet from 2010 to 2020-04-28, it was detected on 2020-11-23 at W1 = 17.99 and W2 = 17.67 AB (about 960 K dust; about 5.6e5 L_sun at 7.9 Mpc) and faded over the following year. Public Hubble images from 2021-02-16 show a point source at the position (F814W = 24.95 AB) that is gone by 2022, and JWST/NIRCam images from 2024 show a new, cooler (about 580 K) dust source there. No optical, radio or X-ray counterpart is known. A normal supernova hidden by dust fits poorly; an obscured luminous red nova, an ILRT-like eruption or a low-energy supernova behind clumpy dust remain possible. JWST spectroscopy of the remnant could decide.

publication_revisions.abstract: We report AT 2020afkm, a dust-obscured mid-infrared transient in NGC 3239 (about 7-12 Mpc), found in a blind difference-imaging search of the unWISE time-resolved coadds of 318 nearby galaxies. Quiet from 2010 to 2020-04-28, it was detected on 2020-11-23 at W1 = 17.99 and W2 = 17.67 AB (about 960 K dust; about 5.6e5 L_sun at 7.9 Mpc) and faded over the following year. Public Hubble images from 2021-02-16 show a point source at the position (F814W = 24.95 AB) that is gone by 2022, and JWST/NIRCam images from 2024 show a new, cooler (about 580 K) dust source there. No optical, radio or X-ray counterpart is known. A normal supernova hidden by dust fits poorly; an obscured luminous red nova, an ILRT-like eruption or a low-energy supernova behind clumpy dust remain possible. JWST spectroscopy of the remnant could decide.
